steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper on answerability in retrieval-augmented open-domain question answering: why models need to abstain when the retrieved text doesn't contain the answer, what is wrong with how existing datasets handle unanswerable questions, and the research questions our study addresses.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- ODQA with retrieval augmentation; abstaining is overlooked
- How Natural Questions handles unanswerable questions
- Shortcoming 1: two kinds of unanswerability mixed together
- Shortcoming 2: no negative samples for training abstention
- Random-excerpt approach and why it is too easy
- Our study: research questions, ChatGPT-generated excerpts

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- ODQA with retrieval augmentation
  - powerful, widely sought-after NLP tool
  - single model has limited memory capacity; knowledge keeps evolving
  - so answers sourced from retrieved text excerpts (Wikipedia, news outlets, etc.)
  - overlooked: what to do when retrieved context isn't enough to answer
  - models trained to always answer can't abstain, forced to guess
  - confounds true model errors with retrieval deficiencies
- Natural Questions (NQ) (cite)
  - widely used ODQA benchmark; designers discuss the issue, include unanswerable questions
  - training instance: question + gold text excerpt + exact answer from excerpt
  - questions from real Google Search queries; annotators find excerpts and answers
  - 50.5% of initial seed: no relevant excerpt found
  - further 14.7%: no straightforward answer from available excerpts (answer present but can't be simply stated per guidelines)
  - kept and labeled unanswerable, to promote study of unanswerability
- Two shortcomings (other ODQA datasets have no unanswerable questions at all)
  - first: unanswerable label conflates (I) no relevant excerpts, (II) answer hard to formulate even with relevant docs
  - we focus on type I: inaccurate retrieval or insufficient corpus knowledge, often the case (cite)
  - second, more important: training models to recognize irrelevant retrieved text
  - retrievers rank documents for a query and return top k, so model always gets one or more excerpts
  - abstention must be trained/evaluated with negative samples
  - type I points in NQ have no negative samples -> unusable in practice
- Random pairing approach (cite)
  - pair questions with excerpts sampled randomly from the NQ pool, label unanswerable
  - very high rates of correct abstention (around 99%)
  - concern: models learn a simple heuristic, e.g. no semantic overlap = abstain
  - real retrieved excerpts likely share semantic content with question but still lack the answer
- This work
  - study predictions on questions paired with semantically related but practically irrelevant excerpts
  - RQ1: which training strategy recognizes such excerpts and abstains efficiently?
  - RQ2: hallucinate vs misguidedly extract; confirmation bias: correct answer mentioned in irrelevant context extracted more often than same-type entities
  - ChatGPT to generate excerpts for each research question

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Open-domain Question Answering (ODQA) systems are a powerful NLP tool that a lot of people want. Because a single model can only remember so much and because knowledge keeps changing, many of these systems use retrieval augmentation, where answers are taken from text excerpts retrieved from reliable sources like Wikipedia, news outlets, etc. There is a lot of research on ODQA, but one thing that is always overlooked is what happens when the retrieved context does not have enough information to answer the question. Models that are trained to always give an answer cannot abstain, so they are forced to guess, and this mixes up real model errors with problems in the retrieval process.

The designers of the Natural Questions (NQ) benchmark, which is now widely used for ODQA, discuss this issue and they include unanswerable questions. A training instance in NQ is generally a question together with a gold-standard text excerpt relevant to the question and an exact answer taken from the excerpt. The questions come from real Google Search queries and annotators were employed to collect relevant text excerpts and to annotate answers. While collecting the data, they found that for 50.5% of the initial seed of questions no relevant text excerpts could be found, and for another 14.7% of the questions no straightforward answer could be formed from the available excerpts. In this second case the excerpts do contain an answer, but it is the kind of answer that cannot simply be stated according to the guidelines. The authors decided to keep these questions in the benchmark and label them as unanswerable, so that unanswerability in ODQA would be studied.

- Two shortcomings (other ODQA datasets have no unanswerable questions at all)
  - first: label conflates (I) no relevant excerpts and (II) answer hard to formulate even with relevant docs
  - focus on type I: inaccurate retrieval or insufficient corpus knowledge, often the case
  - second, more important: models must learn to recognize irrelevant retrieved text
  - retrievers return top k documents, so input always has excerpts -> need negative samples
  - type I points in NQ have none -> unusable in practice
- Random pairing approach from prior work
  - random excerpts from NQ pool labeled unanswerable; ~99% correct abstention
  - concern: simple heuristic (no semantic overlap); real excerpts share semantic content but lack answer
- This work: semantically related but practically irrelevant excerpts
  - RQ1 training strategy for recognizing them and abstaining
  - RQ2 hallucinate vs misguided extraction, confirmation bias
  - ChatGPT generates excerpts per research question

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Open-domain Question Answering (ODQA) systems are a powerful NLP tool that a lot of people want. Because a single model can only remember so much and because knowledge keeps changing, many of these systems use retrieval augmentation, where answers are taken from text excerpts retrieved from reliable sources like Wikipedia, news outlets, etc. There is a lot of research on ODQA, but one thing that is always overlooked is what happens when the retrieved context does not have enough information to answer the question. Models that are trained to always give an answer cannot abstain, so they are forced to guess, and this mixes up real model errors with problems in the retrieval process.

The designers of the Natural Questions (NQ) benchmark, which is now widely used for ODQA, discuss this issue and they include unanswerable questions. A training instance in NQ is generally a question together with a gold-standard text excerpt relevant to the question and an exact answer taken from the excerpt. The questions come from real Google Search queries and annotators were employed to collect relevant text excerpts and to annotate answers. While collecting the data, they found that for 50.5% of the initial seed of questions no relevant text excerpts could be found, and for another 14.7% of the questions no straightforward answer could be formed from the available excerpts. In this second case the excerpts do contain an answer, but it is the kind of answer that cannot simply be stated according to the guidelines. The authors decided to keep these questions in the benchmark and label them as unanswerable, so that unanswerability in ODQA would be studied.

There are two shortcomings in this setup, and it is understandable that they have prevented more study of answerability on NQ (other ODQA datasets do not have unanswerable questions at all). The first is that the unanswerable label in NQ mixes two different challenges in QA: (I) there are no relevant text excerpts for the question, and (II) the special case where an answer cannot easily be formulated even when the documents are very relevant. In this paper we focus on type I unanswerability. This type happens when retrieval systems are inaccurate or the knowledge in the corpus is not sufficient, which can often be the case.

The second shortcoming is more important, and it is about training models to recognize when the retrieved text is irrelevant. Retrieval systems are designed to rank the documents in a database for a query and return the k most relevant ones. So ODQA models always get one or more text excerpts in their input, and this means that their ability to abstain has to be trained and evaluated using some negative samples. The type I data points in NQ do not have such negative samples, so in practice they cannot be used to study unanswerability.

Prior work proposes a simple way to deal with this: questions are paired with text excerpts sampled at random from the whole pool of excerpts associated with NQ, and those questions are labeled unanswerable. When training and evaluating on data points made in this way, they see very high rates of models correctly abstaining (around 99%). Our concern is that models trained like this probably just learn a simple heuristic, where abstaining means noticing that the excerpt has nothing to do with the question, for example because there is no semantic overlap. But in real-world scenarios the retrieved excerpts will probably share semantic content with the question and still not necessarily contain an answer.

In this work we study what models predict when questions are paired with text excerpts that are semantically related but practically irrelevant. We have the following research questions:

- What training strategy can be used to recognize semantically related but practically irrelevant text excerpts efficiently and abstain from answering?

- Are models more likely to hallucinate an answer or to wrongly extract one? This is a kind of confirmation bias, where mentions of the factually correct answer in a practically irrelevant context are extracted more often than entities of the same type in such a context.

We use ChatGPT to automatically generate text excerpts according to a set of criteria for each of the research questions above.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Open-domain Question Answering (ODQA) systems are a powerful and widely sought-after Natural Language Processing tool. Given the limits to the memory capacity of a single model and the ever-evolving nature of knowledge, many such systems rely on retrieval augmentation, where answers are sourced from text excerpts retrieved from reliable sources such as Wikipedia, news outlets, etc. In the large body of research on ODQA, one aspect that is consistently overlooked is how to handle cases where the retrieved context does not provide enough information to answer the given question. Models trained to always provide an answer lack the ability to abstain and are instead forced to guess the answer, which confounds true model errors with deficiencies in the retrieval process.

[1] discuss this issue when designing the now widely used ODQA benchmark Natural Questions (NQ) and include unanswerable questions. The general format of a training instance in NQ is a question paired with a gold-standard text excerpt relevant to the question and an exact answer taken from the text excerpt. The authors source questions from real-world Google Search queries and employ annotators to collect relevant text excerpts and answer annotations. During data collection, they found that no relevant text excerpts could be found for 50.5% of the initial seed of questions, and no straightforward answer could be formed from the available text excerpts for a further 14.7% of the questions – here the text excerpts are said to contain an answer, but one that cannot be simply stated following the guidelines. The authors include these questions in the benchmark, labeling them as unanswerable, to promote the study of unanswerability in ODQA.

Two shortcomings in this data setup have understandably prevented further study of answerability on NQ (and on other ODQA datasets, which do not include unanswerable questions at all). First, the unanswerable label in NQ conflates two types of challenges in QA: (I) the lack of relevant text excerpts for a given question, and (II) the special case of questions for which an answer cannot easily be formulated even with very relevant documents. Here, we focus on type I unanswerability, which arises when retrieval systems are inaccurate or when the knowledge in the corpus is insufficient, as can often be the case [2,3].

Second, and more important, is the question of training models to recognize when the retrieved text is irrelevant. By design, retrieval systems rank the documents in a database with respect to a query and retrieve the k most relevant ones. ODQA models therefore always receive one or more text excerpts as input, so their ability to abstain from answering has to be trained and evaluated with reference to some negative samples. The type I data points in NQ contain no such negative samples, which makes them unusable for the practical study of unanswerability.

[4] propose a simple approach to this issue—pairing questions with text excerpts sampled randomly from the complete pool of excerpts associated with NQ and labeling those questions as unanswerable. When training and evaluating on data points built this way, they observe very high rates of models correctly abstaining from an answer (in the range of 99%). We raise the concern that this approach likely leads models to learn a simple heuristic, where abstaining from an answer amounts to recognizing that the text excerpt has no relevance to the question, for example, based on the lack of semantic overlap. In real-world scenarios, however, retrieved excerpts are likely to share semantic content with the question while still not necessarily containing an answer to it.

In this work, we study the predictions of models faced with questions paired with semantically related but practically irrelevant text excerpts, with the following research questions in mind:

- • What training strategy can achieve high efficiency in recognizing semantically related but practically irrelevant text excerpts and abstaining from providing answers?

- • Are models more likely to hallucinate an answer or misguidedly extract one, falling toward confirmation bias, where mentions of the factually correct answer in a practically irrelevant context are extracted more often than entities of the same type appearing in such a context?

To automatically generate text excerpts according to a given set of criteria, we use ChatGPT to generate text excerpts for each research question above.

References:
[1] Kwiatkowski et al. (2019) Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, and Slav Petrov. 2019. Natural questions: A benchmark for question answering research . Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics , 7:452–466.
[2] Karpukhin et al. (2020) Vladimir Karpukhin, Barlas Oguz, Sewon Min, Patrick Lewis, Ledell Wu, Sergey Edunov, Danqi Chen, and Wen-tau Yih. 2020. Dense passage retrieval for open-domain question answering . In Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) , pages 6769–6781, Online. Association for Computational Linguistics.
[3] Izacard et al. (2022) Gautier Izacard, Mathilde Caron, Lucas Hosseini, Sebastian Riedel, Piotr Bojanowski, Armand Joulin, and Edouard Grave. 2022. Unsupervised dense information retrieval with contrastive learning. Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. , 2022.
[4] Neeman et al. (2022) Ella Neeman, Roee Aharoni, Or Honovich, Leshem Choshen, Idan Szpektor, and Omri Abend. 2022. DisentQA: Disentangling parametric and contextual knowledge with counterfactual question answering .
